desc:
One machine must run jobs, where jobs[i] = [release, work, deadline]. Time is divided into unit slots, slot t being the interval from t to t + 1. In each slot the machine runs at most one job, and job i may only occupy slots t with release ≤ t < deadline. A job may be paused and resumed any number of times, and it needs exactly work slots in total.

Return true if every job can get all its slots, otherwise false.

jobs = [[0, 2, 4], [1, 1, 2]]  ->  true
jobs = [[0, 3, 4], [1, 2, 3]]  ->  false

In the first example the second job takes slot 1 and the first job takes slots 0 and 2. In the second example the second job must use slots 1 and 2, which leaves only slots 0 and 3 for the first job, one short.
hints: Simulate time slot by slot (jumping over idle stretches). At every moment you must decide which of the released, unfinished jobs to run.
Always running the job that is most urgent is the natural choice, and a newly released job may deserve to interrupt the current one.

Earliest Deadline First: keep a heap of (deadline, remaining work) for released jobs; run the top one until it finishes or until the next release, whichever comes first, and report false if a job finishes after its deadline.
editorial: Earliest Deadline First (EDF) with preemption is optimal for feasibility on one machine: if any schedule meets all deadlines, EDF does too. The usual exchange argument shows that if at some slot a feasible schedule runs a job with a later deadline while a released job with an earlier deadline is waiting, swapping a slot of the two keeps both feasible.

Simulating slot by slot is too slow for times up to 107, so jump between events. Sort the jobs by release time. Maintain the time t and a min-heap keyed by deadline of released jobs with remaining work. If the heap is empty, jump to the next release. Otherwise take the top job and run it for min(remaining, next_release - t) units; if it completes, check t ≤ deadline, otherwise push it back with less remaining work (it stays at the top of the heap, since its deadline is unchanged, unless new jobs arrive). Each job is touched O(1) times per release, so the total cost is O(n log n).
solution:
import heapq


def canScheduleAll(jobs):
    jobs = sorted(jobs)
    n = len(jobs)
    heap = []
    t = 0
    i = 0
    INF = 10 ** 18
    while i < n or heap:
        if not heap and t < jobs[i][0]:
            t = jobs[i][0]
        while i < n and jobs[i][0] <= t:
            heapq.heappush(heap, [jobs[i][2], jobs[i][1]])
            i += 1
        nxt = jobs[i][0] if i < n else INF
        deadline, remaining = heap[0]
        run = min(remaining, nxt - t)
        t += run
        if run == remaining:
            heapq.heappop(heap)
            if t > deadline:
                return False
        else:
            heap[0][1] = remaining - run
    return True
